en.title: How to Transfer Inherited Land to the Heirs
en.directAnswer: When a landowner dies, the heirs should first identify the lawful heirs and the property left by the deceased. They then need the required death and inheritance documents and can apply to update the land record. This page explains the record-update process. It does not calculate each heir’s share.

atAGlance.whoFor: Heirs want to update land records after a death.
atAGlance.legalBasis: Applicable personal law; Ministry of Land mutation process; Registration rules where later deeds are made.
atAGlance.mainRule: Inheritance shares depend on the applicable personal law. Do not use this page as an inheritance calculator.
atAGlance.updateStatus: Link this process guide to separate, legally reviewed inheritance guides for share calculations.

en.lawMeaning: Inheritance shares depend on the applicable personal law. Do not use this page as an inheritance calculator. This page gives a general route. A person’s exact rights can change because of facts, documents, deadlines, legal status, court orders or later amendments.
steps: Identify lawful heirs under the applicable law.
Collect heirship or supporting documents required by the authority.
Use a lawful partition or later transfer if heirs want separate ownership.
evidence: Death record; heirship/inheritance documents; deeds; khatian; applicant IDs; tax records; court order if any.
en.simpleExample: Three siblings inherit land. They should not quietly mutate the whole property into one person’s name unless the law and documents support that result.
commonMistakes: Common mistakes: using a family list without legal basis.
Common mistakes: mixing inheritance with sale.
Common mistakes: assuming mutation creates a share that the person did not inherit..

whatIf.question: What if an heir lives abroad?
What if heirs disagree?
whatIf.answer: Do not force a record change that ignores the dispute.

whatIf.question: What if there is a will?
whatIf.answer: Get advice on its legal effect.

en.specialistTrigger: Contested heirs; will dispute; missing documents; minor heirs; property already sold by one person; family disagreement.
